tool.name: SQLAlchemy
tool.tagline: Python's SQL toolkit and ORM: Core expression language plus mapped classes
tool.description: SQLAlchemy is the standard Python library for working with relational databases. Its Core layer builds SQL from Python expressions across PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite and more, and its ORM maps classes to tables with sessions, relationships and a unit of work. It sits under FastAPI, Flask and countless data pipelines, so knowing it well pays off in almost any Python back end.

glossary.def: SQLAlchemy's lower layer: it manages database connections and lets you build SQL statements from Python objects instead of strings.
SQLAlchemy's object for one database: it knows the database's address and driver and keeps a pool of open connections ready to hand out.
A one-line address for a database, written like a website link, e.g. postgresql+psycopg://user:pw@host/db: database system, driver, login, server and database name.
Python's standard shape for database driver libraries (PEP 249). Because every driver follows it, SQLAlchemy can work with any of them.
A named slot in an SQL statement, like :name, whose value is sent separately from the SQL text, so the value can never be mistaken for SQL.
In SQLAlchemy, the component that knows one database's SQL flavour and driver, and turns SQLAlchemy statements into SQL that database accepts.
SQLAlchemy's collection of table descriptions (Table objects). It can create all of those tables in a database with create_all().
A Python class the ORM links to a database table: each instance stands for one row and each mapped attribute for one column.
In SQLAlchemy, the Session object: the ORM's workspace. It keeps track of the objects you load or add and writes their changes to the database inside one transaction.
When the Session sends its waiting changes to the database as INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE statements, inside the open transaction but without committing yet.
The Session flushing waiting changes automatically before it runs a query, so the query sees them.
In SQLAlchemy, to make an object forget its loaded values so they are reloaded from the database the next time you read them. By default, commit() expires every object.
A rule on a relationship for passing an action from one object on to the objects linked to it, such as saving or deleting a user's posts along with the user.
Fetching related rows only when you first touch the relationship attribute, with a separate query at that moment. SQLAlchemy's default.
Fetching related rows up front, together with the main query, instead of one extra query per object later.
A setting added to one query, like selectinload(User.posts), that says how its relationships should be loaded.
An extra table for a many-to-many link: each row pairs one row of one table with one row of the other, through two foreign keys.
A mapped class for an association table, used when the link itself has data, such as a membership's role.
An ORM object whose session has been closed; it still holds its values but can no longer load anything from the database.
One self-contained task, and the pattern of collecting all of its changes and writing them to the database together in the right order.
The session's dictionary of loaded objects, keyed by class and primary key, so each row is represented by exactly one Python object per session.
The schema migration tool for SQLAlchemy: it keeps an ordered history of scripts that change the database's tables and applies them in order.
Alembic's feature that compares your models with the real database and drafts a migration script for the difference, which you then review.
A SQLAlchemy property that runs Python code when read on an object, but builds an SQL expression when used on the class inside a query.
A running process making a copy of itself, the child process, which starts with a copy of the parent's memory, including any open connections.
In SQLAlchemy, turning a statement object built in Python into SQL text plus a list of parameter values, in the dialect of one database.

A small Python package SQLAlchemy uses internally to connect its normal code with async code.

concepts.name: Engines, connections and text()
concepts.summary: Create an Engine, open a Connection, run raw SQL with text() and commit explicitly.
concepts.why: Every SQLAlchemy program starts with an Engine, whether it sends SQL or works with Python objects, and its explicit commits are the basis of all transaction handling.
concepts.body:
Gluing SQL strings together inside Python gets messy fast. **SQLAlchemy** is the most widely used Python library for working with relational databases, and it comes in two layers. **SQLAlchemy Core** sends SQL for you and lets you build statements out of Python objects. On top of it sits the **ORM** (object-relational mapper), which lets you treat each row as an ordinary Python object and saves your changes for you. This course uses the modern "2.0 style" of both.

Everything starts with an **Engine**: one object per database that knows where the database is and how to talk to it. You create it with `create_engine()` and a **database URL**, a one-line address written like a website link. `postgresql+psycopg://user:pw@host/db` names the database system, the driver (explained next), the login, the server and the database name.

A **driver** is a separate Python package that does the actual talking to one kind of database; SQLAlchemy sits on top of it. All Python database drivers follow one standard shape, called the **DBAPI**, which is how SQLAlchemy can work with any of them. SQLite ships with Python, so `sqlite://` needs no extra install.

Opening a connection to a database server is slow, so the Engine keeps a **connection pool**: a few open connections that are handed out and returned, like a stack of cups next to the coffee machine. It doesn't connect at all until you first ask for a connection.

`engine.connect()` borrows a **Connection** from the pool; use it in a `with` block so it goes back at the end. `conn.execute(text("SELECT ..."))` runs SQL. `text()` lets you leave named slots like `:name`, filled from a dict. These are **bound parameters**: the values travel separately from the SQL text, so a name like `O'Brien` can't break the query or sneak in commands. Never paste values into the SQL string yourself.

You decide when changes become permanent. A Connection starts a transaction on first use, and nothing is saved until you call `conn.commit()`; leaving the block without it rolls back. `engine.begin()` commits for you when the block finishes, and rolls back if an exception escapes.

Results are `Row` objects that behave like named tuples: `row.name` or `row[0]`. While learning, pass `echo=True` to `create_engine` to print every SQL statement SQLAlchemy sends.
concepts.code:
from sqlalchemy import create_engine, text

engine = create_engine("sqlite://")  # SQLite kept in memory only

with engine.connect() as conn:
    conn.execute(text("CREATE TABLE users (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT)"))
    conn.execute(text("INSERT INTO users (name) VALUES (:name)"),
                 [{"name": "ada"}, {"name": "linus"}])
    conn.commit()  # without this, the inserts are rolled back

with engine.begin() as conn:  # commits automatically at the end
    conn.execute(text("UPDATE users SET name = 'Ada' WHERE id = :id"), {"id": 1})

with engine.connect() as conn:
    for row in conn.execute(text("SELECT id, name FROM users ORDER BY id")):
        print(row.id, row.name)
# 1 Ada
# 2 linus
takeaways: One Engine per database for the whole program; it owns the connection pool
text() + named :params for raw SQL, never string formatting
connect() needs an explicit commit(); begin() commits for you
Rows behave like named tuples
pitfalls: Forgetting conn.commit() and wondering why the data vanished.
Creating a new Engine for every query, which throws the pool away each time.

quiz.q: You run an INSERT inside `with engine.connect() as conn:` and never call commit(). What happens?
options: It is committed by the next statement
It is committed when the block exits
It is rolled back when the connection is returned
It raises an error at the end of the block
quiz.explain: connect() waits for you to commit: without commit() the transaction is rolled back when the connection goes back to the pool.

concepts.name: Core: MetaData and Table
concepts.summary: Describe tables in Python with MetaData, Table and Column, create them, and build insert and select statements.
concepts.why: Table metadata is what lets SQLAlchemy generate correct SQL for any database instead of hand-written strings.
concepts.body:
In SQLAlchemy Core you describe your schema as Python objects. A **MetaData** object is a collection of table descriptions; each **Table** has a name and **Column**s with types such as `Integer`, `String(50)` or `DateTime`, plus options like `primary_key=True` or `nullable=False`.

With the metadata in place, `metadata.create_all(engine)` runs `CREATE TABLE` for every table that doesn't exist yet. It's handy for tests and prototypes. Real projects change an existing schema with migration scripts (covered in a later lesson), because `create_all` never alters a table that already exists.

The payoff is the **SQL expression language**: instead of writing SQL strings, you build statements from table objects, like `insert(users).values(name="ada")` or `select(users).where(users.c.name == "ada")`. Columns live under `table.c`. Comparing a column with a value gives you a piece of SQL, not `True` or `False`. SQLAlchemy then writes the finished SQL in your database's own SQL dialect, with bound parameters, so quoting and the small differences between databases are handled for you.

- `print(stmt)` shows the SQL a statement will produce, useful when a query doesn't do what you expect.
- `conn.execute(insert(users), [dict, dict])` inserts every dict in the list in one efficient call.
- Results from `select()` are the same `Row` objects you get from `text()`.

Many applications use only Core, especially for reports or moving large amounts of data. If you use the ORM, the classes in the next lesson create these same `Table` objects for you behind the scenes.
concepts.code:
from sqlalchemy import (MetaData, Table, Column, Integer, String,
                        create_engine, insert, select)

metadata = MetaData()
users = Table("users", metadata,
              Column("id", Integer, primary_key=True),
              Column("name", String(50), nullable=False))

engine = create_engine("sqlite://")
metadata.create_all(engine)

with engine.begin() as conn:
    conn.execute(insert(users), [{"name": "ada"}, {"name": "grace"}])

stmt = select(users.c.id, users.c.name).where(users.c.name == "grace")
print(stmt)
# SELECT users.id, users.name
# FROM users
# WHERE users.name = :name_1
with engine.connect() as conn:
    print(conn.execute(stmt).all())  # [(2, 'grace')]
takeaways: MetaData holds Table objects; Columns carry types and constraints
Columns live under table.c and comparisons build SQL expressions
create_all creates missing tables but never alters existing ones
print(stmt) shows the generated SQL
pitfalls: Relying on create_all to apply schema changes to an existing database.

quiz.q: What does `users.c.name == 'ada'` evaluate to in Python?
options: A SQL expression object used in a WHERE clause
quiz.explain: SQLAlchemy gives == a special meaning on columns: instead of True or False it builds an expression object that becomes name = :param in the SQL.

concepts.name: ORM models with Mapped and mapped_column
concepts.summary: Map Python classes to tables with DeclarativeBase, Mapped[] annotations and mapped_column().
concepts.why: Declarative models are how nearly all modern SQLAlchemy ORM code defines its data.
concepts.body:
The ORM maps a **class** to a table and its **instances** to rows. Such a class is called a **mapped class**, or simply a model. You first create one shared base class by subclassing `DeclarativeBase`; every model then subclasses that base and sets `__tablename__` to its table's name.

Columns are declared with **`Mapped[...]` type annotations**, which set both the Python type and the database column:

- `id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)` is an integer primary key.
- `name: Mapped[str]` alone is enough for a `NOT NULL` string column.
- `Mapped[Optional[str]]` or `Mapped[str | None]` makes the column **nullable**: allowed to hold NULL.
- `mapped_column(String(50), unique=True, index=True)` adds a specific type and constraints.

Python types map to SQL types automatically (`int` to `Integer`, `str` to `String`, `datetime` to `DateTime`, `Decimal` to `Numeric`). For default values, `default=` gives one computed in Python, while `server_default=func.now()` asks the database itself to fill in the current time (`func` builds calls to SQL functions).

Behind the scenes each class gets a Core `Table`, available as `User.__table__`, and the base has a shared `Base.metadata`, so `Base.metadata.create_all(engine)` works exactly as in Core.

Instances are plain Python objects. SQLAlchemy writes an `__init__` for you that accepts the columns as keyword arguments, so `User(name="ada")` just works. Creating one doesn't touch the database; saving it is covered in the next lesson.

Adding a `__repr__` makes objects print readably. Type checkers such as mypy understand `Mapped[]`, so they know `user.name` is a `str`.
concepts.code:
from datetime import datetime
from typing import Optional
from sqlalchemy import String, func, create_engine
from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, mapped_column

class Base(DeclarativeBase):
    pass

class User(Base):
    __tablename__ = "users"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    email: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(String(120), unique=True)
    nickname: Mapped[Optional[str]]
    created: Mapped[datetime] = mapped_column(server_default=func.now())

    def __repr__(self) -> str:
        return f"User({self.id!r}, {self.email!r})"

engine = create_engine("sqlite://")
Base.metadata.create_all(engine)
print(User.__table__.c.keys())  # ['id', 'email', 'nickname', 'created']
print(User(email="a@x.io"))     # User(None, 'a@x.io'): no id until saved
takeaways: Subclass DeclarativeBase once; every model inherits from it
Mapped[T] sets the Python type and nullability; mapped_column() adds SQL details
Optional[...] makes a column nullable, otherwise NOT NULL
Each model has a Core Table at Model.__table__
pitfalls: Expecting the id to be set right after User(...): the database assigns it only when the object is saved.

quiz.q: How do you declare a nullable text column `bio` in a 2.0-style model?
quiz.explain: Optional in the Mapped annotation tells SQLAlchemy the column is nullable.

concepts.name: The Session: add, commit and get
concepts.summary: Use a Session to add objects, commit them to the database and load them back by primary key.
concepts.why: Every save and every load of ORM objects goes through a Session, so this is the core loop of all ORM code.
concepts.body:
A **Session** is the ORM's workspace. It holds a connection and a transaction, keeps track of the objects you load or add, and writes their changes to the database. Think of a shopping cart: you put objects in, and nothing is final until you check out with `commit()`.

The basic cycle:

- `session.add(obj)` or `session.add_all([...])` puts new objects in the session, waiting to be saved.
- `session.commit()` first **flushes**: it sends the waiting changes to the database as INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE statements. Then it commits the transaction.
- `session.get(User, 5)` loads a row by primary key, or returns `None` if there's no such row. If that object is already in the session, you get it back without a query.

Use the Session in a `with` block so it's closed at the end. In a real program you call `sessionmaker(engine)` once; it returns a factory, here `SessionLocal`, that makes new sessions all set up the same way. Open a short-lived session for each separate task, such as each page a website serves or each run of a job.

After `commit()`, by default every object is **expired**: SQLAlchemy forgets its loaded values and reloads them from the database the next time you read an attribute. That guarantees fresh data, but it surprises people who read objects after the session is closed, because then there's nothing to reload from. Set `expire_on_commit=False` on the sessionmaker when you need to return objects from a function after committing.

If something fails, `session.rollback()` throws away the transaction; leaving the `with` block without committing also rolls back.
concepts.code:
from sqlalchemy import create_engine
from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, mapped_column, sessionmaker

class Base(DeclarativeBase):
    pass

class User(Base):
    __tablename__ = "users"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    name: Mapped[str]

engine = create_engine("sqlite://")
Base.metadata.create_all(engine)
SessionLocal = sessionmaker(engine)

with SessionLocal() as session:
    ada = User(name="ada")
    session.add_all([ada, User(name="linus")])
    session.commit()
    print(ada.id)              # 1: the database assigned it during the flush

with SessionLocal() as session:
    print(session.get(User, 2).name)  # linus
    print(session.get(User, 99))      # None
takeaways: add() stages objects; commit() flushes and commits
session.get(Model, pk) loads by primary key or returns None
Create a sessionmaker once, open short-lived sessions from it
Objects are expired after commit unless expire_on_commit=False
pitfalls: Keeping one global Session for the whole program instead of a fresh one per task.

quiz.q: What does session.get(User, 42) return when no row has id 42?
quiz.explain: get() returns None for a missing primary key instead of raising an exception.

concepts.name: Querying with select() and scalars()
concepts.summary: Build ORM queries with select(Model), run them through the session, and pick the result method that says how many rows you expect.
concepts.why: This is the modern query style that replaced the older session.query(), and every read in an ORM program goes through it.
concepts.body:
In 2.x the same `select()` construct serves Core and ORM. `select(User)` selects entire `User` objects; `select(User.name, User.id)` selects individual columns. Model attributes like `User.name` act like `table.c.name`, so `select(User).where(User.name == "ada")` reads naturally.

Run it through the session:

- `session.execute(stmt)` returns a `Result` of `Row`s. For `select(User)` each row is a one-element tuple holding a User.
- `session.scalars(stmt)` keeps just the first value of each row (a single value like this is called a **scalar**), so you iterate over `User` objects directly. This is what you want when you select one kind of object.
- `session.scalar(stmt)` returns the first value or `None`.

The result offers methods that state your expectation:

- `.all()` gives a list.
- `.first()` gives the first item or `None` (add `.limit(1)` to the statement so the database doesn't do extra work).
- `.one()` requires exactly one row and raises `NoResultFound` or `MultipleResultsFound` otherwise.
- `.one_or_none()` allows zero.

Prefer `one()` when a missing row is a bug: it fails loudly instead of returning `None`.

The older `session.query(User).filter(...)` still works, but new code should use `select()`. Statements are immutable: `stmt.where(...)` returns a new statement and leaves the original alone, which makes it easy to build queries step by step.
concepts.code:
from sqlalchemy import create_engine, select
from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, mapped_column, Session

class Base(DeclarativeBase):
    pass

class User(Base):
    __tablename__ = "users"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    name: Mapped[str]

engine = create_engine("sqlite://")
Base.metadata.create_all(engine)
with Session(engine) as s:
    s.add_all([User(name="ada"), User(name="bob"), User(name="cy")])
    s.commit()

    users = s.scalars(select(User).order_by(User.name)).all()
    print([u.name for u in users])                     # ['ada', 'bob', 'cy']
    print(s.execute(select(User)).first())             # (<__main__.User ...>,)
    print(s.execute(select(User.id, User.name)).all()[0])  # (1, 'ada')
    bob = s.scalars(select(User).where(User.name == "bob")).one()
    print(bob.id)                                      # 2
takeaways: select(User) for objects, select(User.a, User.b) for columns
session.scalars() to get objects; execute() returns Rows
.one() / .one_or_none() / .first() / .all() state how many rows you expect
Statements are immutable: .where() returns a new one
pitfalls: Using session.execute(select(User)) and getting 1-tuples instead of User objects.

quiz.q: Which call returns a list of User objects for stmt = select(User)?
quiz.explain: scalars() unwraps the single entity column; execute() would give Row tuples.

concepts.name: Filtering, ordering and limits
concepts.summary: Combine where() conditions with and_/or_, in_, like and is_(None), then sort and page with order_by, limit and offset.
concepts.why: Real queries are mostly about narrowing and ordering rows correctly, and SQLAlchemy's operators differ from plain Python in a few key places.
concepts.body:
`where()` accepts any number of SQL expressions, joined with AND. Calling `.where()` again adds more conditions. Column attributes support Python operators that SQLAlchemy turns into SQL: `==`, `!=`, `<`, `>=`.

Some SQL operators need methods instead, because Python doesn't let a library change what its keywords `and`, `or`, `not` and `in` do:

- `User.id.in_([1, 2, 3])` and `.not_in(...)`.
- `User.name.like("a%")`, `.ilike(...)` for case-insensitive matching, `.startswith("a")`, `.contains("x")`.
- `User.email.is_(None)` becomes `IS NULL`; `== None` works too, but code-checking tools flag it as a likely mistake.
- `or_(a, b)`, `and_(a, b)`, `not_(a)` from `sqlalchemy`; the bitwise `|`, `&` and `~` operators work as well, but mind their precedence and wrap comparisons in parentheses.
- `User.age.between(18, 30)`.

Never use Python `and`, `or`, `not` or `in` on columns: they try to evaluate truthiness and raise or silently produce the wrong query.

Sort with `order_by(User.name)`, `User.created.desc()` or `.nulls_last()`. Page with `.limit(20).offset(40)`. Offset pagination gets slow on large tables because the database still walks the skipped rows; for big lists, "keyset" pagination (`where(User.id > last_seen_id).order_by(User.id).limit(20)`) is faster and stable.
concepts.code:
from sqlalchemy import create_engine, select, or_
from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, mapped_column, Session

class Base(DeclarativeBase):
    pass

class User(Base):
    __tablename__ = "users"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    name: Mapped[str]
    age: Mapped[int | None]

engine = create_engine("sqlite://")
Base.metadata.create_all(engine)
with Session(engine) as s:
    s.add_all([User(name=n, age=a) for n, a in
               [("ada", 36), ("alan", 41), ("bob", None), ("cy", 19)]])
    s.commit()
    q = (select(User.name)
         .where(or_(User.name.like("a%"), User.age.is_(None)))
         .order_by(User.name.desc()).limit(2))
    print(s.scalars(q).all())                                   # ['bob', 'alan']
    print(s.scalars(select(User.name).where(User.id.in_([1, 4]))).all())  # ['ada', 'cy']
takeaways: Chained or multiple where() conditions are ANDed
Use in_(), like(), is_(None), between() for SQL operators
or_/and_/not_ (or |, &, ~ with parentheses), never Python and/or/not
Prefer keyset pagination over large offsets
pitfalls: Writing `User.age > 18 and User.age < 30`: Python's `and` breaks the expression.

quiz.q: How do you express `name IN ('a', 'b')`?
quiz.explain: Python doesn't let libraries change what the in keyword does, so SQLAlchemy provides the in_() method.

concepts.name: Updating and deleting
concepts.summary: Change objects by setting attributes, delete them with session.delete(), or run bulk update() and delete() statements.
concepts.why: Knowing when to modify objects and when to issue one bulk statement is the difference between clean code and thousands of needless queries.
concepts.body:
With the ORM you update rows by **changing attributes** on loaded objects. The Session notices the change (the object becomes "dirty") and emits an `UPDATE` for just the modified columns at the next flush or commit. There's no `save()` call.

To remove a row, call `session.delete(obj)`; the `DELETE` runs at flush. Later you'll see how deleting one object can also delete the objects linked to it.

Loading every object just to change one field is wasteful for many rows. For bulk changes, run a single UPDATE or DELETE statement through the session:

- `session.execute(update(User).where(User.active == False).values(status="archived"))`
- `session.execute(delete(User).where(User.last_login < cutoff))`

These run one SQL statement regardless of row count. Objects already loaded in the session are kept in sync where possible: by default the ORM evaluates the WHERE clause in Python against loaded objects (`synchronize_session="auto"`). The result's `rowcount` tells you how many rows matched.

Bulk statements skip the ORM's per-object work: no objects are loaded, so any Python logic you attached to individual objects never runs. Use them for plain data changes. Either way, the changes are only permanent after `commit()`.
concepts.code:
from sqlalchemy import create_engine, select, update, delete
from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, mapped_column, Session

class Base(DeclarativeBase):
    pass

class User(Base):
    __tablename__ = "users"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    name: Mapped[str]
    active: Mapped[bool] = mapped_column(default=True)

engine = create_engine("sqlite://")
Base.metadata.create_all(engine)
with Session(engine) as s:
    s.add_all([User(name="ada"), User(name="bob"), User(name="cy")])
    s.commit()
    ada = s.get(User, 1)
    ada.name = "Ada"                # dirty: UPDATE at next flush
    s.delete(s.get(User, 3))        # DELETE at next flush
    r = s.execute(update(User).where(User.name == "bob").values(active=False))
    print(r.rowcount)               # 1
    s.commit()
    print(s.execute(select(User.name, User.active)).all())
    # [('Ada', True), ('bob', False)]
takeaways: Change attributes on loaded objects; the Session emits UPDATE at flush
session.delete(obj) removes a row at flush
update()/delete() statements change many rows in one SQL statement
Bulk statements skip the ORM's per-object logic
pitfalls: Looping over 100,000 loaded objects to set a flag instead of one update() statement.

quiz.q: You load a User and set user.name = 'x'. What else is needed to persist it?
quiz.explain: Loaded objects are tracked; the change is flushed as an UPDATE when you commit.

concepts.name: relationship() and one-to-many
concepts.summary: Link models with a ForeignKey column plus relationship() on both sides using back_populates, and control cascades.
concepts.why: Relationships let you work with user.posts instead of hand-joining ids, and their cascade settings decide what happens on save and delete.
concepts.body:
A database link needs a **foreign key column** on the "many" side: `user_id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(ForeignKey("users.id"))`. The ORM adds **`relationship()`** attributes on top so you can navigate between objects:

- On `User`: `posts: Mapped[list["Post"]] = relationship(back_populates="author")`.
- On `Post`: `author: Mapped["User"] = relationship(back_populates="posts")`.

The `Mapped[list[...]]` annotation makes it a collection: one user has many posts, a **one-to-many** link. A plain class makes it a single object: each post has one author (many-to-one). `back_populates` names the attribute on the other side and keeps both sides in sync in Python: appending a post to `user.posts` sets `post.author`, before anything is flushed.

A **cascade** is a rule for passing an action on from one object to the objects linked to it. Thanks to the default "save-update" cascade, adding the user to the session adds its posts too, and the foreign key values are filled in at flush time. You never set `post.user_id` by hand.

Deletion needs a decision. By default, deleting a user sets `user_id` to NULL on its posts (which fails if the column is NOT NULL). Use `cascade="all, delete-orphan"` on the parent's collection when children can't exist without their parent: deleting the user deletes its posts, and removing a post from `user.posts` deletes it.

Relationships use **lazy loading** by default: the related rows are fetched only when you first touch them, so reading `user.posts` on a loaded user runs a SELECT at that moment. Loading strategies are covered in their own lesson.
concepts.code:
from sqlalchemy import ForeignKey, create_engine, select
from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, mapped_column, relationship, Session

class Base(DeclarativeBase): pass
class User(Base):
    __tablename__ = "users"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    name: Mapped[str]
    posts: Mapped[list["Post"]] = relationship(back_populates="author",
                                               cascade="all, delete-orphan")
class Post(Base):
    __tablename__ = "posts"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    title: Mapped[str]
    user_id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(ForeignKey("users.id"))
    author: Mapped[User] = relationship(back_populates="posts")

engine = create_engine("sqlite://"); Base.metadata.create_all(engine)
with Session(engine) as s:
    ada = User(name="ada", posts=[Post(title="Engines"), Post(title="Notes")])
    s.add(ada)                       # posts cascade in automatically
    s.commit()
    print(ada.posts[0].author.name, ada.posts[0].user_id)   # ada 1
    s.delete(ada); s.commit()
    print(s.scalars(select(Post)).all())                   # []
takeaways: ForeignKey column on the many side, relationship() on both sides
back_populates keeps both directions in sync in Python, before saving
Related objects are added via save-update cascade; FK values are set at flush
cascade='all, delete-orphan' when children belong to the parent
pitfalls: Setting the foreign key id by hand and the relationship as well, then getting confused when they disagree.

quiz.q: Without delete cascade, what does deleting a User do to its Posts by default?
quiz.explain: The default cascade unlinks children by setting their foreign key to NULL, which fails if the column is NOT NULL.

concepts.name: Joins in select()
concepts.summary: Join related tables in a select() with join() along relationships or explicit ON clauses, including outer joins.
concepts.why: Filtering or reporting across tables needs SQL joins, and SQLAlchemy can infer the ON clause from your relationships.
concepts.body:
`select(User).join(User.posts)` joins along a relationship, and SQLAlchemy derives the `ON users.id = posts.user_id` clause from the mapping. You can also join to a model class, which SQLAlchemy calls an **entity**: `.join(Post)`, and SQLAlchemy finds the foreign key; or give an explicit condition, `.join(Post, Post.user_id == User.id)`, when there are several or no foreign keys between the tables.

The join lets you filter and select on the joined table: `select(User.name, Post.title).join(User.posts).where(Post.title.like("%SQL%"))`. Note that joining does **not** load the relationship collection; it only makes the other table available in the query. Filling the collection is a separate job, covered in a later lesson.

- `.outerjoin(User.posts)` or `.join(..., isouter=True)` keeps users without posts, with NULLs for post columns.
- `.select_from(Post).join(Post.author)` sets the left side explicitly when the first selected entity isn't where the join should start.
- Joining the same table twice requires an **alias**: `a = aliased(User)`.

Joining a one-to-many relationship multiplies rows: a user with three posts appears three times. If you select only `User` objects, the ORM returns duplicates of the same object; use `.distinct()`, or an `EXISTS` filter (`User.posts.any(Post.title == "x")`), which keeps a user once if at least one matching post exists.
concepts.code:
from sqlalchemy import ForeignKey, create_engine, select
from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, mapped_column, relationship, Session

class Base(DeclarativeBase): pass
class User(Base):
    __tablename__ = "users"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    name: Mapped[str]
    posts: Mapped[list["Post"]] = relationship()
class Post(Base):
    __tablename__ = "posts"

    title: Mapped[str]
    user_id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(ForeignKey("users.id"))

                    .where(Post.title.like("%SQL%"))).all())   # [('ada', 'SQL tips')]
    print(s.execute(select(User.name, Post.title).outerjoin(User.posts)
        .order_by(User.name, Post.title)).all())  # [('ada', 'Joins'), ('ada', 'SQL tips'), ('bob', None)]

outerjoin keeps rows with no match
Joining does not load the relationship collection
.any() / .has() produce EXISTS filters without duplicating rows

quiz.q: What does `select(User).join(User.posts)` do to user.posts?
options: Fills it with the joined posts
Nothing: it only makes posts available for filtering
Turns it into a list of tuples
quiz.explain: Joins affect the SQL rows; filling collections is done separately, with options covered later.

concepts.name: Aggregates, group_by and labels
concepts.summary: Count, sum and group rows with func, group_by and having, and name result columns with label().
concepts.why: Dashboards and reports are aggregations, and doing them in SQL is far faster than loading objects into Python.
concepts.body:
SQL functions come from the `func` object: `func.count()`, `func.sum(Order.total)`, `func.avg(...)`, `func.max(...)`, `func.lower(User.name)`. Any name works (`func.date_trunc(...)`) and becomes a call to the SQL function of that name, so database-specific functions are available too.

Grouping looks like SQL: `select(User.name, func.count(Post.id)).join(User.posts).group_by(User.name)`. Every selected column must be grouped or aggregated. `.having(func.count(Post.id) > 2)` filters groups after aggregation, while `.where()` filters rows before it.

Give computed columns a name with `.label("n_posts")`. The label becomes the attribute name on result rows (`row.n_posts`) and can be reused in `order_by`, either as the label object or by name string.

For single numbers, `session.scalar(select(func.count()).select_from(User))` counts rows; note `select_from`, because `func.count()` alone doesn't mention a table. To count the rows a filtered query returns, wrap it as a **subquery** (a query used inside another query): `select(func.count()).select_from(stmt.subquery())`.

Aggregates return Rows, not ORM objects. Combine with an outer join to include zero counts: count a column from the outer side (`func.count(Post.id)`), because `count(*)` would count the NULL row as 1.
concepts.code:
from sqlalchemy import ForeignKey, create_engine, select, func
from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, mapped_column, relationship, Session

class Base(DeclarativeBase): pass
class User(Base):
    __tablename__ = "users"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    name: Mapped[str]
    posts: Mapped[list["Post"]] = relationship()
class Post(Base):
    __tablename__ = "posts"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    user_id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(ForeignKey("users.id"))

engine = create_engine("sqlite://")
Base.metadata.create_all(engine)
with Session(engine) as s:
    s.add_all([User(name="ada", posts=[Post(), Post(), Post()]),
               User(name="bob", posts=[Post()]), User(name="cy")])

    stmt = select(User.name, n).outerjoin(User.posts).group_by(User.name).order_by(n.desc())

        print(row.name, row.n_posts)   # ada 3 / bob 1 / cy 0
    print(s.scalar(select(func.count()).select_from(User)))   # 3
takeaways: func.<name>() calls any SQL function
where() filters rows, having() filters groups
.label('x') names a result column for row.x and order_by
Count a column from the outer-joined side to get zeros
pitfalls: Using count(*) with an outer join, which counts 1 for parents with no children.

quiz.q: Which clause filters groups by an aggregate like count > 2?
quiz.explain: Aggregates are computed after WHERE, so conditions on them go in HAVING.

concepts.name: Many-to-many and association objects
concepts.summary: Model many-to-many links with a secondary association table, or an association object when the link has its own data.
concepts.why: Tags, roles, memberships and enrollments are all many-to-many, and choosing the right pattern up front avoids painful rewrites later.
concepts.body:
A post can have many tags and a tag can label many posts: a many-to-many link. It needs an **association table**, an extra table where each row links one post to one tag through two foreign keys. If the link carries no extra data, define it as a plain Core `Table` and pass it as `secondary`:

`tags: Mapped[list["Tag"]] = relationship(secondary=post_tags, back_populates="posts")`

The ORM then manages the association rows for you: `post.tags.append(tag)` inserts a row, removing the tag deletes it. You never map the association table as a class.

When the link has its own columns, like a membership's `role` or `joined_at`, use an **association object** instead: map the association table as a class (`Membership`) with a many-to-one relationship to each side, and give each side a one-to-many relationship to `Membership`. You then create `Membership(user=u, group=g, role="admin")` explicitly. To keep a convenient `user.groups` view as well, the `association_proxy` helper can give you the groups directly, skipping the Membership objects in between.

Make the association table's primary key the pair of foreign keys so the same link can't be stored twice. Deleting a Post removes its rows from a `secondary` table automatically; deleting the tags themselves is up to you.

Starting with the simple `secondary` form and later needing link data means a schema migration and code changes, so ask early whether the relationship itself has attributes.
concepts.code:
from sqlalchemy import Column, ForeignKey, Table, create_engine, select
from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, mapped_column, relationship, Session

class Base(DeclarativeBase): pass
post_tags = Table("post_tags", Base.metadata,
    Column("post_id", ForeignKey("posts.id"), primary_key=True),
    Column("tag_id", ForeignKey("tags.id"), primary_key=True))
class Post(Base):
    __tablename__ = "posts"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    title: Mapped[str]
    tags: Mapped[list["Tag"]] = relationship(secondary=post_tags, back_populates="posts")
class Tag(Base):
    __tablename__ = "tags"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    name: Mapped[str]
    posts: Mapped[list[Post]] = relationship(secondary=post_tags, back_populates="tags")

engine = create_engine("sqlite://"); Base.metadata.create_all(engine)
with Session(engine) as s:
    py, db = Tag(name="python"), Tag(name="db")
    s.add_all([Post(title="ORM", tags=[py, db]), Post(title="Pandas", tags=[py])]); s.commit()
    print(sorted(p.title for p in py.posts))                # ['ORM', 'Pandas']
    print(s.scalars(select(Post.title).join(Post.tags).where(Tag.name == "db")).all())  # ['ORM']
takeaways: secondary=<Table> for plain many-to-many links
The ORM inserts and deletes association rows as you edit the lists
Use an association object class when the link has its own columns
Make the two foreign keys the association table's primary key
pitfalls: Adding a column to a secondary table and finding there is no way to set it through the relationship.

quiz.q: A user can belong to many groups and each membership has a role. Which pattern fits?
options: A JSON column of group ids
Two one-to-many relationships without a link table
quiz.explain: Link data like role needs its own mapped class; secondary tables can't expose extra columns.

concepts.name: Transactions, flush and session lifecycle
concepts.summary: Understand flush versus commit, use session.begin() blocks, handle rollback, and scope sessions correctly in applications.
concepts.why: Most real-world ORM bugs (outdated values, half-written changes, DetachedInstanceError) come from misunderstanding when the session talks to the database.
concepts.body:
A Session always works inside a transaction. **Flush** sends pending changes to the database as SQL, inside that transaction, so later queries in the same session see them; **commit** flushes and then makes everything permanent. Statements executed through the session **autoflush** (flush automatically) first by default (in 2.1, any statement, including `text()`), which is why a just-added object shows up in a `select()` before you commit. `session.flush()` is also how you get a database-generated id without committing.

Two idiomatic shapes:

- `with Session(engine) as s:` ... `s.commit()` for explicit commits.
- `with Session(engine) as s, s.begin():` (or `with SessionLocal.begin() as s:`) commits when the block ends and rolls back on an exception.

If a flush fails (say, an IntegrityError because a UNIQUE constraint was violated), the session's transaction is broken: you must call `rollback()` before using that session again. A rollback also expires all objects so they reload from the database.

**Scope**: one session per **unit of work**, meaning one self-contained task. On a website's server that is one session per incoming visitor action, opened when it arrives and closed when the reply is sent; a web framework (a library for building websites, like Flask or FastAPI) usually does this for you. Don't share a session between threads, parts of one program running at the same time: a Session isn't built for that.

Objects move through states: transient (just created), pending (added, not yet flushed), persistent (saved as a row and tracked by a session) and **detached** (its session has closed). Lazy-loading or refreshing a detached object raises `DetachedInstanceError`, which is why returning ORM objects out of a closed session needs care.
concepts.code:
from sqlalchemy import create_engine, select
from sqlalchemy.exc import IntegrityError
from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, mapped_column, sessionmaker

class Base(DeclarativeBase): pass
class User(Base):
    __tablename__ = "users"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    email: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(unique=True)

engine = create_engine("sqlite://"); Base.metadata.create_all(engine)
SessionLocal = sessionmaker(engine)
with SessionLocal.begin() as s:          # commits at the end of the block
    u = User(email="a@x.io"); s.add(u)
    s.flush()                            # INSERT sent, still uncommitted
    print(u.id)                          # 1

with SessionLocal() as s:
    try:
        s.add(User(email="a@x.io")); s.commit()   # duplicate email
    except IntegrityError:
        s.rollback()                     # required before reusing the session
        print("duplicate")
    print(s.scalar(select(User.email)))  # a@x.io
takeaways: flush sends SQL inside the transaction; commit makes it permanent
Queries autoflush pending changes first
After a failed flush, rollback() before reusing the session
One session per unit of work, never shared across threads
pitfalls: Catching an IntegrityError and continuing to use the session without rollback().

quiz.q: After session.flush() but before commit(), who can see the inserted row?
options: Other sessions too, after a short delay
quiz.explain: The flush executes the INSERT inside the session's still-open transaction, visible to that transaction.

concepts.name: Loading strategies and the N+1 problem
concepts.summary: Avoid N+1 queries by choosing selectinload, joinedload or raiseload for relationships instead of default lazy loading.
concepts.why: Lazy loading in a loop is the most common ORM performance bug, turning one page view into hundreds of queries.
concepts.body:
By default relationships use **lazy loading**: `user.posts` runs a SELECT the first time you touch it. Fine for one object, terrible in a loop. Listing 100 users and their posts costs 1 query for users plus 100 for posts: the **N+1 query** problem.

The fix is **eager loading**: fetching the related rows up front, together with the main query. You ask for it per query with **loader options**:

- `selectinload(User.posts)` runs one extra query, `SELECT ... WHERE posts.user_id IN (...)`, for all loaded users. Best default for collections.
- `joinedload(Post.author)` adds a LEFT OUTER JOIN to the same query. Best for many-to-one; for collections it multiplies rows, and you must call `.unique()` on the result.
- `raiseload("*")` makes any unloaded relationship access raise, which catches accidental lazy loads in tests and in code that must stay fast.

Chain options for nested paths: `selectinload(User.posts).selectinload(Post.comments)`. You can also set a default strategy on the relationship itself, `relationship(lazy="selectin")`, if you almost always need it.

When you already join for filtering, `contains_eager(User.posts)` tells the ORM to populate the collection from the joined rows instead of querying again; just note the collection then contains only the rows your filter kept.

Lazy loading also fails outright once an object's session has closed, so explicit loading is a good habit everywhere. Turn on `echo=True` and count queries to spot N+1 early.
concepts.code:
from sqlalchemy import ForeignKey, create_engine, select, event
from sqlalchemy.orm import (DeclarativeBase, Mapped, mapped_column, relationship,
                            Session, selectinload)

class Base(DeclarativeBase): pass
class User(Base):
    __tablename__ = "users"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    posts: Mapped[list["Post"]] = relationship()
class Post(Base):
    __tablename__ = "posts"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    user_id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(ForeignKey("users.id"))

engine = create_engine("sqlite://"); Base.metadata.create_all(engine)
queries = []
event.listen(engine, "before_cursor_execute", lambda *a: queries.append(1))
with Session(engine) as s:
    s.add_all([User(posts=[Post(), Post()]) for _ in range(10)]); s.commit()
    queries.clear()
    for u in s.scalars(select(User)): len(u.posts)            # lazy
    print(len(queries))                                         # 11
    s.expire_all(); queries.clear()
    for u in s.scalars(select(User).options(selectinload(User.posts))): len(u.posts)
    print(len(queries))                                         # 2
takeaways: Default lazy loading = one query per object when used in a loop (N+1)
selectinload for collections, joinedload for many-to-one
raiseload catches accidental lazy loads
contains_eager reuses a join you already wrote
pitfalls: joinedload on a collection without .unique() on the result.
Fixing N+1 globally with lazy='joined' everywhere and making every query huge.

quiz.q: Listing 50 orders and printing order.customer.name triggers 51 queries. Best fix?
quiz.explain: An eager loader option fetches all customers in the same or one extra query, removing the per-row lazy loads.

concepts.name: Schema migrations with Alembic
concepts.summary: Version your schema with Alembic: init, autogenerate revisions from your models, review them and upgrade or downgrade.
concepts.why: Your database keeps its data while your code changes release after release, so schema changes must be scripted, reviewed and applied in order on every copy of the database.
concepts.body:
**Alembic** is SQLAlchemy's migration tool, from the same authors. `alembic init migrations` creates an `alembic.ini` settings file and a `migrations/` folder holding `env.py` and a `versions/` folder. In `env.py`, set `target_metadata = Base.metadata` so Alembic knows your models, and put your database URL in `alembic.ini`.

Each migration is a Python file with `upgrade()` and `downgrade()` functions using `op.add_column`, `op.create_table`, `op.create_index` and friends. Files are chained by `revision` and `down_revision` ids, forming an ordered history; the database stores its current revision in an `alembic_version` table.

The everyday loop:

- Change your models.
- `alembic revision --autogenerate -m "add user bio"` compares your models with the real database and writes a migration file for the difference; this is called **autogenerate**.
- **Read and edit** the generated file. Autogenerate can't detect renames (it sees a drop plus an add, losing data), and misses some changes like certain server defaults or constraint changes.
- `alembic upgrade head` applies pending migrations; `alembic downgrade -1` steps back.

Data migrations (backfilling a new column) go in the same files using `op.execute(...)` or Core statements on `op.get_bind()`. For large tables, add nullable columns first, backfill, then add the NOT NULL constraint in a later migration to avoid long locks. Run migrations once as a separate release step, not every time the app starts: you may be running many copies of the app at once.
concepts.code:
# migrations/versions/3f2a_add_user_bio.py  (generated, then reviewed)
from alembic import op
import sqlalchemy as sa

revision = "3f2a"
down_revision = "9c1e"

def upgrade() -> None:
    op.add_column("users", sa.Column("bio", sa.Text(), nullable=True))
    op.create_index("ix_users_email", "users", ["email"], unique=True)

def downgrade() -> None:
    op.drop_index("ix_users_email", table_name="users")
    op.drop_column("users", "bio")

# $ alembic revision --autogenerate -m "add user bio"
# $ alembic upgrade head
# $ alembic current        -> 3f2a (head)
takeaways: Set target_metadata = Base.metadata in env.py for autogenerate
Always review autogenerated migrations, especially renames
upgrade head to apply, downgrade -1 to step back
Split risky changes: add nullable, backfill, then constrain
pitfalls: Trusting autogenerate for a column rename, which drops the column and its data.

quiz.q: You rename the model attribute and column `name` to `full_name` and run autogenerate. What will it usually produce?
options: A drop of name and an add of full_name
quiz.explain: Autogenerate can't infer intent, so a rename looks like one column removed and another added.

concepts.name: Subqueries, CTEs and window functions
concepts.summary: Compose queries with .subquery(), .cte(), scalar_subquery() and over() for window functions.
concepts.why: Reports like 'latest order per customer' or running totals need subqueries and windows, and SQLAlchemy builds them from reusable pieces.
concepts.body:
Any `select()` can become a building block:

- `.subquery()` turns it into a derived table you can join to or select from. Its columns live under `.c`, like a Table.
- `.cte("name")` does the same as a `WITH` clause, which reads better for multi-step queries. `.cte(recursive=True)` plus `union_all` builds a recursive CTE, one that refers to itself, for walking trees like an org chart.
- `.scalar_subquery()` makes a one-value subquery usable as a column or in a comparison, e.g. a count of each customer's orders shown on every row. When it mentions a table of the outer query, SQLAlchemy automatically links it to the outer query's current row, making it a correlated subquery.

**Window functions** use `.over()` on a function: `func.row_number().over(partition_by=Order.customer_id, order_by=Order.created.desc())`, or `func.sum(Order.total).over(order_by=Order.created)` for a running total. Windows can't appear in WHERE, so the classic "top 1 per group" is a window in a subquery or CTE, filtered outside.

To get ORM objects back from a subquery, use `aliased(Order, subq)`, which maps the entity onto the subquery's columns. Then `select(alias)` returns `Order` instances.

Build complex queries in named steps, print them to check the SQL, and remember each step is immutable and reusable.
concepts.code:
from sqlalchemy import create_engine, select, func
from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, mapped_column, Session

class Base(DeclarativeBase): pass
class Order(Base):
    __tablename__ = "orders"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    customer: Mapped[str]
    total: Mapped[int]

engine = create_engine("sqlite://"); Base.metadata.create_all(engine)
with Session(engine) as s:
    s.add_all([Order(customer=c, total=t) for c, t in
               [("ada", 30), ("ada", 50), ("bob", 20), ("bob", 70), ("bob", 10)]])
    s.commit()
    ranked = select(Order.customer, Order.total,
                    func.row_number().over(partition_by=Order.customer,
                                           order_by=Order.total.desc()).label("rn")
                    ).cte("ranked")
    top = select(ranked.c.customer, ranked.c.total).where(ranked.c.rn == 1)
    print(s.execute(top.order_by(ranked.c.customer)).all())  # [('ada', 50), ('bob', 70)]
    avg = select(func.avg(Order.total)).scalar_subquery()
    print(s.scalars(select(Order.id).where(Order.total > avg)).all())  # [2, 4]
takeaways: subquery() and cte() turn a select into a table-like object with .c
scalar_subquery() gives a single value usable in expressions
func.x().over(partition_by=..., order_by=...) for window functions
aliased(Model, subq) maps ORM entities onto a subquery
pitfalls: Trying to filter on a window function in the same query's WHERE clause.

quiz.q: How do you keep only the top-ranked row per group computed with row_number().over(...)?
options: Put the window in a subquery or CTE and filter outside it
quiz.explain: Window functions are evaluated after WHERE and HAVING, so the filter must wrap the windowed query.

concepts.name: Async SQLAlchemy
concepts.summary: Use create_async_engine and AsyncSession with an async driver, and never let lazy loading run a hidden query.
concepts.why: Async web frameworks like FastAPI serve many visitors at once and must never sit idle waiting on the database, and async SQLAlchemy has rules the normal ORM doesn't.
concepts.body:
**Asynchronous** (async) code, which you met with `async` and `await`, lets one program start a database call and serve other work while it waits for the answer. The `sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio` extension wraps the same Core and ORM in versions you `await`. Install it with `pip install "sqlalchemy[asyncio]"`, which adds the greenlet package (a helper SQLAlchemy uses internally to connect its normal code with async code), plus an async driver: `postgresql+asyncpg://`, `mysql+aiomysql://` or `sqlite+aiosqlite://`.

- `engine = create_async_engine(url)`; `async with engine.begin() as conn:` for Core work, and `await conn.run_sync(Base.metadata.create_all)` to call sync-only helpers.
- `async_sessionmaker(engine, expire_on_commit=False)` creates `AsyncSession`s. Disabling expire-on-commit matters more here, because reloading an expired attribute would need a hidden database call.
- Every operation that talks to the database is awaited: `await session.execute(stmt)`, `await session.scalars(stmt)`, `await session.get(User, 1)`, `await session.commit()`. `session.add()` is not awaited; it only stages.

The big rule: **no hidden I/O**. Every database call must be awaited, and a plain attribute access can't be. So touching a lazy-loaded relationship raises `MissingGreenlet` instead of running a query. Load what you need up front with `selectinload`, or use `lazy="raise"` to find mistakes; the `AsyncAttrs` mixin also offers `await obj.awaitable_attrs.posts` for an explicit async load.

One `AsyncSession` per task: it's not safe to use concurrently from multiple coroutines, so `asyncio.gather` over one session is a bug. Call `await engine.dispose()` at shutdown.
concepts.code:
import asyncio
from sqlalchemy import select
from sqlalchemy.ext.asyncio import create_async_engine, async_sessionmaker
from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, mapped_column

class Base(DeclarativeBase): pass
class User(Base):
    __tablename__ = "users"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    name: Mapped[str]

async def main():
    engine = create_async_engine("sqlite+aiosqlite://")
    async with engine.begin() as conn:
        await conn.run_sync(Base.metadata.create_all)
    Session = async_sessionmaker(engine, expire_on_commit=False)
    async with Session() as s:
        s.add_all([User(name="ada"), User(name="bob")])   # no await: just staging
        await s.commit()
        names = (await s.scalars(select(User.name).order_by(User.name))).all()
        print(names)                                        # ['ada', 'bob']
    await engine.dispose()

asyncio.run(main())
takeaways: Async engine + async driver (asyncpg, aiosqlite) + AsyncSession
Await execute/scalars/get/commit; add() is not awaited
No lazy loading: eager-load relationships or use awaitable_attrs
One AsyncSession per task; never share it across concurrent coroutines
pitfalls: Touching user.posts in async code and getting MissingGreenlet.
Running asyncio.gather on several queries using the same AsyncSession.

quiz.q: Why is expire_on_commit=False usually recommended for AsyncSession?
options: Accessing expired attributes after commit would need a hidden database call, which async code can't make
quiz.explain: Expired attributes reload on access; in async code that hidden query raises an error instead of running.

concepts.name: Hybrid properties and computed columns
concepts.summary: Define attributes that work both on instances and in queries with hybrid_property, and use column_property for SQL-computed values.
concepts.why: Keeping logic like full_name or is_overdue in one place, usable in Python and in WHERE clauses, avoids duplicated rules.
concepts.body:
A Python **property** is a method you read like an attribute, without parentheses, made with `@property`. A **`hybrid_property`** is a property that works two ways: on an instance it runs your Python code, but read on the class it builds a SQL expression. So `user.full_name` returns a string and `User.full_name == "Ada L"` works inside `where()`.

If the Python body also works on columns (string concatenation, arithmetic, comparisons), one function covers both. When it doesn't, for example it uses an `if`, Python-only functions or `len()`, add a separate SQL version with `@full_name.inplace.expression` (or the older `@full_name.expression`), returning an expression built from class attributes, often with `case()` or `func`.

Hybrids can also have setters (`@x.inplace.setter`) to split a value into columns.

Related tools:

- `column_property(select(...).scalar_subquery())` adds a read-only attribute loaded with the object via SQL, like a comment count. It's computed in every query that loads the entity, so use `deferred=True` for expensive ones.
- `Computed("price * qty")` declares a database-generated column, stored or virtual depending on the database.
- Plain `@property` is fine when you never query on the value.

Hybrids are evaluated in Python for loaded objects and in SQL in queries, so make sure both paths agree, especially around NULL handling.
takeaways: hybrid_property works on instances (Python) and on the class (SQL)
Add an .inplace.expression when the Python logic can't be turned into SQL
column_property for SQL-computed attributes loaded with the object
Keep the Python and SQL versions consistent, including NULLs
pitfalls: Using Python `if` in a hybrid without an expression version, so queries silently use the wrong branch or error.

quiz.q: Why does the example define a separate expression for status?
options: Expressions are required for all hybrids
Hybrids can't be read on instances
The Python version uses an if statement, which can't be turned into SQL
quiz.explain: On the class, self.balance < 0 is a SQL expression and if would test its truthiness, so a case() version is needed.

concepts.name: Connection pooling and engine tuning
concepts.summary: Configure the engine's QueuePool (pool_size, max_overflow, pool_pre_ping, pool_recycle) and handle forked processes and serverless setups.
concepts.why: Pool settings decide whether your app survives database restarts, connections dropped after sitting unused, and sudden bursts of traffic.
concepts.body:
An Engine keeps a **pool** of DBAPI connections so each piece of work doesn't pay to connect. The default for most databases is `QueuePool`:

- `pool_size=5`: connections kept open.
- `max_overflow=10`: extra connections allowed under load, closed when returned.
- `pool_timeout=30`: seconds to wait for a free connection before raising `TimeoutError`, which usually means sessions are being held too long or leaked.
- `pool_pre_ping=True`: test a connection with a lightweight ping on checkout and replace it if the server dropped it (after a restart, or a switch to another server). Cheap insurance; recommended.
- `pool_recycle=1800`: replace connections older than this many seconds, for databases or network middlemen that silently close connections left unused for a while (MySQL's `wait_timeout`, cloud load balancers).

Size the pool against the database's connection limit. Each running copy of your program, a **process**, has its own pool, so `(pool_size + max_overflow) x processes` must fit. **Serverless** functions (code a cloud provider starts on demand, maybe hundreds of copies at once) make this worse. There, use a separate pooling program like PgBouncer, which shares a few real connections among many clients, and `poolclass=NullPool` in the app.

**Forking** is a process copying itself into a child process, open connections included. Servers like Gunicorn and job runners like Celery fork their workers, and a copied connection must never be used by two processes. Create the engine after the fork, or call `engine.dispose(close=False)` in the child so it starts with a fresh pool.

`engine.pool.status()` shows checked-in and checked-out counts, handy when the pool keeps running out.
concepts.code:
from sqlalchemy import create_engine, text
from sqlalchemy.pool import QueuePool

engine = create_engine(
    "sqlite:///app.db",
    poolclass=QueuePool,   # explicit here; the default for server databases
    pool_size=5,
    max_overflow=10,
    pool_timeout=30,
    pool_pre_ping=True,    # replace dead connections transparently
    pool_recycle=1800,     # recycle connections older than 30 minutes
)
with engine.connect() as conn:
    conn.execute(text("SELECT 1"))
    print(engine.pool.checkedout())   # 1
print(engine.pool.checkedout())       # 0: returned to the pool
print(engine.pool.status())
# Pool size: 5  Connections in pool: 1 Current Overflow: -4 Current Checked out connections: 0
takeaways: pool_size + max_overflow cap how many connections one process holds at once
pool_pre_ping handles connections dropped by the server
pool_recycle beats servers that close unused connections
After fork, dispose the inherited pool or create the engine in the child
pitfalls: Sharing an engine's pooled connections between a parent process and its forked children.

quiz.q: Requests hang and then fail with a pool TimeoutError, while the database is idle. Most likely cause?
options: Sessions or connections are not being closed and returned
quiz.explain: Leaked or long-held checkouts exhaust pool_size + max_overflow, so new requests wait for a connection.

concepts.name: Bulk inserts and upserts
concepts.summary: Load many rows fast with insert() and lists of dicts, use RETURNING, and upsert with on_conflict_do_update.
concepts.why: Imports, nightly syncs and data-loading jobs need fast writes and insert-or-update behaviour that adding objects one by one can't deliver.
concepts.body:
Adding thousands of ORM objects with `session.add_all()` works, but the session does bookkeeping for every single object. For bulk loads, pass a **list of dicts** to an insert statement: `session.execute(insert(User), [{"name": "a"}, {"name": "b"}, ...])`. SQLAlchemy groups the rows into a few multi-row INSERT statements, and still applies Python-side column defaults.

Add `.returning(User.id)` to get generated keys back, or `insert(User).returning(User)` to get ORM objects, on databases that support `RETURNING`, an SQL clause that sends back values from the rows just written (PostgreSQL, SQLite, MariaDB, SQL Server).

An **upsert** inserts a row, or updates it if one with the same key already exists. Each database writes it differently, so import `insert` from that database's module in `sqlalchemy.dialects`:

- PostgreSQL and SQLite: `insert(...).on_conflict_do_nothing(index_elements=[...])` or `.on_conflict_do_update(index_elements=["email"], set_={"name": stmt.excluded.name})`. `excluded` refers to the row you tried to insert.
- MySQL and MariaDB: `.on_duplicate_key_update(name=stmt.inserted.name)`.

For bulk updates by primary key, `session.execute(update(User), [{"id": 1, "name": "x"}, ...])` runs the UPDATE once per dict, in one efficient call.

Split very large loads into chunks of a few thousand rows per statement and commit periodically so a single transaction doesn't grow unbounded. Bulk statements skip per-object ORM work, such as saving or deleting linked objects for you.
concepts.code:
from sqlalchemy import create_engine, select, insert
from sqlalchemy.dialects.sqlite import insert as sqlite_insert
from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, mapped_column, Session

class Base(DeclarativeBase): pass
class User(Base):
    __tablename__ = "users"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    email: Mapped[str] = mapped_column(unique=True)
    name: Mapped[str]

engine = create_engine("sqlite://"); Base.metadata.create_all(engine)
with Session(engine) as s:
    rows = [{"email": f"u{i}@x.io", "name": f"user{i}"} for i in range(1000)]
    ids = s.scalars(insert(User).returning(User.id), rows).all()
    print(len(ids), ids[:3])                       # 1000 [1, 2, 3]

    stmt = sqlite_insert(User).values(email="u0@x.io", name="Renamed")
    stmt = stmt.on_conflict_do_update(index_elements=["email"],
                                      set_={"name": stmt.excluded.name})
    s.execute(stmt); s.commit()
    print(s.scalar(select(User.name).where(User.id == 1)))  # Renamed
takeaways: session.execute(insert(Model), list_of_dicts) for fast bulk inserts
.returning() gets generated ids back from the same statement
Upserts use the database-specific insert: on_conflict_do_update / on_duplicate_key_update
Chunk huge loads and commit periodically
pitfalls: Using the generic sqlalchemy.insert and looking for on_conflict_do_update, which only exists on the database-specific inserts.

quiz.q: In on_conflict_do_update, what does stmt.excluded.name refer to?
options: The name value from the row you tried to insert
quiz.explain: EXCLUDED is PostgreSQL/SQLite's name for the proposed row that hit the conflict.

concepts.name: Unit of work and the identity map
concepts.summary: How the Session tracks object state, orders flushes by dependency, and guarantees one object per row through the identity map.
concepts.why: Knowing what the Session does at flush time explains surprising queries, ordering errors, outdated values and memory growth in long sessions.
concepts.body:
The Session implements the **unit of work** pattern: collect every change during a task, then write them all at once in a sensible order. To collect changes, SQLAlchemy **instruments** mapped classes: each mapped attribute is replaced by a Python descriptor, a hook object that runs on every read and write. It records changes in each instance's `InstanceState` (visible via `inspect(obj)`), including the original value of modified attributes. At flush, the session gathers new, dirty and deleted objects and computes the SQL needed.

The flush orders operations by their dependencies between tables and relationships (a topological sort): parents are inserted before children so foreign keys can be filled in, and children deleted before parents. Within a table, rows are grouped into one executemany call (one statement, many parameter sets) where possible. Cyclic dependencies (two rows pointing at each other) need `post_update=True` on one relationship, which issues a second UPDATE after the inserts.

The **identity map** is the session's dictionary of loaded objects, keyed by `(class, primary key)`. It holds them through weak references, so an unchanged object you no longer use can be freed. Loading the same row twice in one session returns the **same Python object**, and `session.get()` returns it with no SQL at all. The flip side: a query that returns rows for objects already in the map does not overwrite their unflushed changes and, by default, does not refresh their loaded attributes. Use `populate_existing()`, `session.refresh(obj)` or `expire()` when you need fresh database values.

Long-running sessions accumulate state; the session holds strong references to dirty and new objects until flush. For batch jobs, commit and `expunge_all()` or use fresh sessions per chunk.
concepts.code:
from sqlalchemy import create_engine, select, inspect, text
from sqlalchemy.orm import DeclarativeBase, Mapped, mapped_column, Session

class Base(DeclarativeBase): pass
class User(Base):
    __tablename__ = "users"
    id: Mapped[int] = mapped_column(primary_key=True)
    name: Mapped[str]

engine = create_engine("sqlite://"); Base.metadata.create_all(engine)
with Session(engine) as s:
    s.add(User(name="ada")); s.commit()
    a = s.get(User, 1)
    b = s.scalars(select(User).where(User.name == "ada")).one()
    print(a is b)                                   # True: identity map
    a.name = "Ada"
    print(inspect(a).attrs.name.history)           # History(added=['Ada'], unchanged=(), deleted=['ada'])
    s.commit(); print(a.name)                       # Ada (reloaded after commit)
    s.execute(text("UPDATE users SET name = 'changed'"))  # behind the ORM's back
    print(s.get(User, 1).name)                      # Ada: identity map, no refresh
    print(s.scalars(select(User).execution_options(populate_existing=True)).one().name)  # changed
takeaways: Instrumented attributes record changes; flush turns them into SQL
Flush order follows dependencies: parents inserted first, deleted last
Identity map: one object per (class, pk) per session
Queries don't refresh already-loaded objects unless asked (populate_existing, refresh)
pitfalls: Expecting a re-query to show changes made by raw SQL or another program to objects already in the session.

quiz.q: You load User 1, then another process changes its name, then you run select(User) in the same session. What does user.name show?
options: The value already loaded, unless you expire, refresh or use populate_existing
quiz.explain: The identity map keeps the existing object's loaded state; fresh values need an explicit refresh.

concepts.name: SQL compilation, dialects and caching
concepts.summary: How statements compile to dialect SQL, how the statement cache works, and how to inspect compiled SQL and parameters.
concepts.why: Understanding compilation helps you check the SQL SQLAlchemy generates, keep its statement cache effective and write constructs that work across databases.
concepts.body:
A `select()` is a tree of `ClauseElement` objects. Before running it, SQLAlchemy **compiles** the tree, turning it into SQL text plus a list of parameter values. That's the job of the engine's **dialect**, the component that knows one database's SQL flavour and driver: its `SQLCompiler` visits each node and emits SQL text with the right quoting, parameter style (`?`, `%(name)s`, `$1`) and syntax (LIMIT vs TOP, RETURNING support). `stmt.compile(dialect=postgresql.dialect())` shows what a given database would receive, and `compile_kwargs={"literal_binds": True}` writes the values straight into the SQL so you can read it; never run SQL built that way from values a user typed in.

Compiling is slow in Python, so each engine keeps a **compiled cache**: a store of SQL it has already produced, reused instead of compiled again. Each statement produces a cache key, a summary of its structure, with bound values left out, so the same query shape with different parameters reuses the compiled form. `echo=True` prints `[cached since 12.3s ago]` or `[generated in 0.0003s]` per statement, telling you whether caching works.

Things that defeat the cache: building SQL strings with values via `text()` f-strings, ever-changing `IN` lists written straight into the SQL text, or custom constructs with `inherit_cache` not set. Third-party `ClauseElement` subclasses must declare `inherit_cache = True` (if safe) or they disable caching with a warning.

The **dialect** also handles type conversion: `bind_processor` and `result_processor` per type turn Python values into driver values and back. Extending compilation for your own construct is done with `@compiles(MyElement, "postgresql")`.
concepts.code:
from sqlalchemy import Table, Column, Integer, String, MetaData, select
from sqlalchemy.dialects import postgresql, mssql

users = Table("users", MetaData(),
              Column("id", Integer, primary_key=True), Column("name", String))
stmt = select(users.c.name).where(users.c.id > 5).limit(3)

print(stmt.compile(dialect=postgresql.dialect()))
# SELECT users.name
# FROM users
# WHERE users.id > %(id_1)s::INTEGER
#  LIMIT %(param_1)s::INTEGER
print(stmt.compile(dialect=mssql.dialect()))
# SELECT TOP __[POSTCOMPILE_param_1] users.name ...
c = stmt.compile(compile_kwargs={"literal_binds": True})
print(" ".join(str(c).split()))       # SELECT users.name FROM users WHERE users.id > 5 LIMIT 3

k1 = select(users).where(users.c.id == 1)._generate_cache_key()
k2 = select(users).where(users.c.id == 2)._generate_cache_key()
print(k1.key == k2.key)               # True: same shape, different parameters
takeaways: Statements are trees compiled per dialect into SQL text plus parameters
The compiled cache keys on statement structure, not bound values
echo=True shows whether each statement was cached or generated
Custom constructs need @compiles and inherit_cache
pitfalls: Formatting values into text() strings, which defeats both caching and the protection bound parameters give against malicious input.

quiz.q: Why do select(users).where(users.c.id == 1) and ... == 2 share one compiled cache entry?
options: The second query is never compiled
They don't; each value is cached separately
The cache key reflects the statement's structure; the values are bound parameters
quiz.explain: Literal values become bound parameters excluded from the cache key, so the compiled SQL is reused.

concepts.name: Custom types and events
concepts.summary: Extend SQLAlchemy with TypeDecorator for custom column types and event listeners that hook into the engine, session and ORM.
concepts.why: Encryption, JSON shapes, time zone rules, auditing and keeping each customer's rows apart are usually built with custom types and events.
concepts.body:
A **TypeDecorator** wraps an existing type and converts values on the way in and out. Set `impl` to the underlying type, implement `process_bind_param(value, dialect)` (Python to database) and `process_result_value(value, dialect)` (database to Python), and set `cache_ok = True` if the type's settings are safe to include in SQLAlchemy's cache of compiled statements. Common uses: forcing timezone-aware UTC datetimes, storing enums or small value objects as strings, transparent encryption.

Mutation tracking is a classic gotcha: if your type stores a dict or list, in-place changes (`obj.data["k"] = 1`) are not detected, because the attribute wasn't reassigned. Wrap the type with `MutableDict.as_mutable(...)` or reassign the value.

**Events** let you register a function, an event listener, that SQLAlchemy calls at a given moment. Use `event.listen(target, "name", fn)` or the `@event.listens_for` decorator:

- Engine/connection: `before_cursor_execute` (logging, query counting), `connect` (per-connection setup like SQLite `PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON`).
- Mapper: `before_insert`, `before_update` per object, e.g. timestamps.
- Session: `before_flush` to inspect `session.new`, `session.dirty` and `session.deleted` (auditing), `after_commit`.
- ORM execute: `do_orm_execute` to rewrite every ORM query, e.g. a filter that limits every query to the current customer's rows, with `with_loader_criteria`.

Listeners run right inside the flush or execution, which waits for them, so keep them fast and avoid emitting new flushes from within flush events.
takeaways: TypeDecorator: impl + process_bind_param + process_result_value
Set cache_ok = True when the type is safe to cache
In-place changes to dict/list columns need Mutable* wrappers
Engine, mapper, session and ORM-execute events hook into every layer
pitfalls: Mutating a JSON dict in place and finding the change never got saved.

quiz.q: You do doc.meta['k'] = 2 on a plain TypeDecorator JSON column and commit. What is saved?
quiz.explain: The attribute was never reassigned, so the session doesn't see it as dirty unless the type is Mutable-wrapped.
